claims.claim: About 3 in 10 older people admitted to an acute hospital leave less able to do basic daily activities (washing, dressing, using the toilet, eating, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking) than they were before they became ill.
claims.supporting_passage: "Random effects meta-analysis showed the combined prevalence across studies was 30% (95% CI: 24%, 36%; p<0.001). Sensitivity analysis of only studies assessing ADL decline from 2 weeks prior to admission to discharge or within a month of discharge showed a combined prevalence of 33% (95% CI: 26%, 41%;)." ... "Prevalence among all hospital-based studies ranged from 17% to 61%" ... "The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) describes functional impairments in activities as having a limitation in independent execution of daily tasks including self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)."
claims.location: Full text, Results (Prevalence of Hospital-Associated Disability) and Introduction; abstract Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ in medical-surgical acute care (15 studies, n=7,375, 1983 to 2013, mostly US); exposure acute hospital stay; outcome loss of independence in basic ADL (modified Katz or Barthel) from before or at admission to discharge or shortly after; no comparator (prevalence).
claims.safe_wording: About 3 in 10 older people who go into an acute hospital come out less able to wash, dress, use the toilet, eat, or get in and out of bed or a chair than they were before they became ill. When only studies that asked about the person's abilities 2 weeks before admission were counted, the figure was about 1 in 3.
claims.qualifications: Pooled estimate from studies that varied widely (17% to 61%); mostly US; data from 1983 to 2013. Measures basic self-care, not tasks such as making tea or using a key. Some of the loss starts with the illness before admission, not only in hospital; do not say the hospital stay caused it. Quote the percentage, not the confidence interval (abstract and full text give different upper limits).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High heterogeneity and possible publication bias among small studies (authors' funnel plots). Brown 2016 trial (cognitively intact veterans, median stay 3 days) found no significant ADL change after discharge in either arm, so the proportion is lower in fitter, shorter-stay groups.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence of hospital-associated disability, 15 studies, 7,375 people aged 65+, acute care
pooled prevalence when restricted to studies with a baseline 2 weeks before admission (8 studies)

claims.claim: Loss of daily abilities after a hospital stay is more common the older the person.
claims.supporting_passage: "Thirty-five percent of patients declined in ADL function between baseline and discharge." ... "The frequency of ADL decline between baseline and discharge varied markedly with age (23%, 28%, 38%, 50%, and 63% in patients aged 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, and > or =90, respectively, P <.001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: 2,293 medical inpatients aged 70+, two US hospitals (1990s); baseline 2 weeks before admission; outcome decline in any of five basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, toileting) at discharge; crude proportions by age band.
claims.safe_wording: In one large US study of people aged 70 and over admitted with a medical illness, about 1 in 4 of those aged 70 to 74 left hospital less able to manage basic self-care than 2 weeks before admission, rising to about 6 in 10 of those aged 90 or over.
claims.qualifications: One cohort, 1990s US data; crude age-band percentages; outcome measured at discharge only.

claims.claim: The first-hour tasks (door key, front step, toilet, chair, kettle, bed) make a practical pre-discharge check; the toilet, chair and bed are the kinds of task the hospital-disability studies measured, while the key, step and kettle go beyond them.
claims.supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)". Covinsky 2003: "interviewed about their independence in five ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, and toileting)".
claims.location: Loyd full text, Introduction; Covinsky abstract, Methods
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition of the basic ADL items used in the evidence.
claims.safe_wording: Present the six tasks as a practical checklist to ask about, not as a tested tool. Getting to and using the toilet, getting up from a chair and getting into bed are basic daily activities that studies of hospital-associated disability count; the key, the front step and the kettle are extra, everyday tasks the post suggests adding.
claims.qualifications: The first-hour framing and the checklist are judgement. No study tested this checklist. Do not claim that asking these questions prevents readmission or harm.

claims.claim: Occupational therapists can assess how a person manages at home, including by a home visit before discharge; families can ask whether this has happened.
claims.supporting_passage: "To determine the effectiveness of pre-discharge home assessment visits by occupational therapists in assisting hospitalized patients from a range of settings to return to community living." ... "There is low-to-moderate quality evidence that pre-discharge home assessment visits reduce patients' risk of falling and increase participation. The risk of readmission to hospital is also reduced, but not for patients following stroke." ... "There was no effect on activity or quality of life."
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospitalised patients (geriatric, mixed rehabilitation and stroke settings); pre-discharge OT home assessment visits versus none or usual care; falls, participation, readmission, activity, quality of life; 14 studies.
claims.safe_wording: Ask the ward therapist whether they have seen your relative do each of these tasks. If something has not been tried, ask whether it can be practised before discharge, whether equipment is needed, and whether an occupational therapist should look at the home.
claims.qualifications: A home visit is not needed or offered for everyone; do not say every hospital provides one or that NICE requires one (NICE NG27 could not be opened). If the evidence is mentioned, say 'low to moderate quality evidence' and that it did not improve daily activity or quality of life.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence quality low to moderate; no effect on activity or quality of life; readmission benefit not seen after stroke.

numbers.meaning: studies in the review

claims.claim: Of older people who leave hospital after a medical illness less able to look after themselves than before, about 3 in 10 are back to their usual level a year later, about 3 in 10 are alive but have not recovered, and about 4 in 10 have died.
claims.supporting_passage: "By 12 months after discharge, among those discharged with new or additional ADL disability, 41.3% died, 28.6% were alive but had not recovered to baseline function, and 30.1% were at their baseline function. Among those discharged with baseline function, 17.8% died, 15.2% were alive but with worse than baseline function, and 67% were at their baseline function(p<.001)." Full text: "Out of 2,279 patients who were eligible for this analysis, 1,480 patients were discharged with similar or better functional status compared to 2 weeks prior to admission while 799 patients were discharged with worse functional status".
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Setting and Participants)
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients 70+ admitted non-electively to general medical services, two Ohio hospitals, 1993 to 1998; exposure discharged with new or additional disability in 5 self-care ADLs versus discharged at baseline (2 weeks before admission); outcomes death, not recovered, recovered at 12 months; crude proportions.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of people aged 70 and over admitted in an emergency with a medical illness (1993 to 1998), 799 of 2,279 left hospital needing more help with washing, dressing, eating, the toilet or moving from bed to chair than 2 weeks before admission. A year later, about 30 in 100 of them were back to their usual level, about 29 in 100 were alive but still needed more help, and about 41 in 100 had died. Among people who left hospital at their usual level, 67 in 100 were still at that level a year later.
claims.qualifications: Old US data; lengths of stay have shortened since (authors' limitation). Deaths reflect how ill this group was; present them plainly and without drama, and say that for some people this decline marks the end of life (the authors recommend considering palliative care alongside rehabilitation).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hardy and Gill 2004 found much higher recovery rates after disability episodes in the community (any cause), so figures depend on setting and cause.

claims.claim: Among people discharged with new loss of self-care, being back to their usual level one month after discharge is linked with a much better outlook at a year.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among patients discharged with a new or additional disability in self-care ADL, the presence or absence of recovery by one month was associated with long-term outcomes. Among those who had recovered by one month after discharge, 56.2% remained at baseline function 1 year after discharge, 20.7% died, and 23.1% declined again in self-care ADL function (). In contrast, among those who did not recover by one month after hospital discharge, only 17.1% recovered baseline function at 1 year after discharge, 44.4% died, and 38.4% were alive but not recovered (p<.001)."
claims.location: Full text, Results (Role of One-Month Outcomes in Predicting Long-term Outcomes); analysis sample n=651
claims.pico_timeframe: 651 of the 799 discharged with new disability who were alive with data at 1 month; exposure recovered to baseline self-care by 1 month versus not; outcomes at 12 months; crude proportions, prognostic association.
claims.safe_wording: In that study, people who were back to their usual self-care one month after leaving hospital did much better over the year: 56 in 100 were still at their usual level at 12 months. Of those not back to their usual level at one month, 17 in 100 had recovered by 12 months.
claims.qualifications: The study measured being back to the usual level by one month, not whether recovery had 'started'; do not say 'started to recover'. Prognostic association only; it does not show that a review at one month improves outcomes. Nearly a quarter of those recovered at one month later declined again.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial found showing that a scheduled one-month review changes outcomes (not specifically searched beyond this check).

claims.claim: Not being back to normal at one month does not rule out recovery: many recoveries happen later.
claims.supporting_passage: "Among those who had a new or additional disability in self-care ADL at hospital discharge, 30% recovered and were at their baseline level of functioning at 1 year. Of these patients, 62% recovered by 1 month with the remainder recovering over the next 11 months. Thus, most recovery, when it happens, occurs in the first month after hospitalization. However, 38% of patients who recovered in the year following discharge do so after the first month after hospitalization." Conclusion: "Since outcomes in the first month seem to predict long-term outcomes, particularly aggressive interventions may be indicated in the first month. However, as a large number of patients may recover after one month, and many who recover by one month decline again, there may also be a need for sustained long-term interventions."
claims.location: Full text, Results (Timing of Functional Recovery) and Conclusion
claims.pico_timeframe: Same cohort; timing of recovery among those at baseline at 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: Of the people who were back to their usual level a year after discharge, about 6 in 10 had got there within the first month and about 4 in 10 got there later. So the one-month point is a useful time to check progress, not a final verdict.
claims.qualifications: Same cohort limitations (US, 1990s). The one-month review is the post's judgement, informed by the authors' conclusion; mark it as a suggestion.

numbers.meaning: of those recovered at 12 months, recovered by 1 month
of those recovered at 12 months, recovered after 1 month

claims.claim: Among community-living people aged 70 and over who became newly disabled (any cause), most regained independence within a year, but recovery was often short-lived; frail, cognitively impaired or severely disabled people recovered less often, although most still did.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 420 participants (56%) experienced disability during a median follow-up of 51 months. Of these participants, 399 (81%) recovered (ie, regained independence in all 4 ADLs) within 12 months of their initial disability episode, and a majority (57%) of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Among participants who experienced 3 or more consecutive months of disability, a majority (60%) recovered, but only a third of these maintained independence for at least 6 months. Persons who were cognitively impaired, physically frail, or severely disabled (ie, in 3-4 ADLs) at onset were less likely to recover than those who were cognitively intact, nonfrail, or mildly disabled, respectively. Nonetheless, a majority of participants within each subgroup recovered."
claims.pico_timeframe: 754 initially non-disabled community-living people 70+, New Haven, 1998 to 2003; exposure new disability (needing personal help with bathing, dressing, walking or transferring) from any cause; outcome regained independence within 12 months, and duration.
claims.safe_wording: In a US community study, 81 in 100 older people who became newly dependent (from any cause) regained independence within a year, but only 57 in 100 of those who recovered stayed independent for at least 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Not a post-hospital cohort; do not place its 81% beside Boyd's 30% as if they were the same group. If used at all, label it as disability arising in the community from any cause. Recommend leaving it out of a post about discharge.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Boyd 2008 discussion: post-hospital prognosis is 'substantially worse than that observed among community-dwelling elders with disability arising from a broad range of causes'.

numbers.meaning: newly disabled people who regained independence within 12 months of first episode
of those who recovered, stayed independent at least 6 months
recovered after 3 or more consecutive months of disability; only a third of these stayed independent 6 months

claims.claim: Older people in hospital spend most of the day lying in bed, including many who can walk.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2009: "Forty-five male patients (mean age 74.2) with a mean length of stay of 5.1 days generated 2,592 one-hour periods of data. A baseline functional assessment indicated that 35 (77.8%) study patients were willing and able to walk a short distance independently. No patient remained in bed the entire measured hospital stay, but on average, 83% of the measured hospital stay was spent lying in bed. The average amount of time that any one individual spent standing or walking ranged from a low of 0.2% to a high of 21%, with a median of 3%, or 43 minutes per day." Pedersen 2013: "The ambulatory patients were lying median 17 hours, (interquartile range [IQR]: 14.4-19.1), sitting 5.1 hours (IQR: 2.9-7.1), and standing and/or walking 1.1 hours (IQR: 0.6-1.7) per day."
claims.location: Brown 2009 Abstract, Results; Pedersen 2013 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Brown: 45 male medical inpatients 65+ able to walk before admission, one US VA hospital, first 7 days, accelerometers. Pedersen: 43 older medical patients able to walk independently, Copenhagen, accelerometers throughout stay.
claims.safe_wording: Older people in hospital spend most of the day in bed, even many who can walk. In a US veterans' hospital, 45 men aged 65 and over spent on average 83% of their measured time lying in bed; the typical time standing or walking was 43 minutes a day, although 35 of the 45 were able to walk a short distance on their own. In a Danish hospital, 43 older medical patients who could walk spent a typical 17 hours a day lying down and about 1 hour standing or walking.
claims.qualifications: Two small single-hospital studies; Brown 2009 is men only. Always name the setting with the figure. Pick one headline figure for the visual (judge's advice).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: C01-B2 notes other small accelerometer studies with lower lying times; figures vary by setting and method. The same Brown 2009 and Pedersen figures are used for C01-05 (falls rate angle); coordinate to avoid repeating the statistic as the lead in both posts.

numbers.meaning: average share of measured hospital time lying in bed, 45 men 65+, first 7 days, one US VA hospital
time standing or walking, Brown 2009
willing and able to walk a short distance independently at baseline, Brown 2009
time lying, 43 ambulatory older medical patients, Denmark
time standing or walking, Pedersen 2013

claims.claim: Low mobility in hospital is linked with worse daily functioning at discharge and a month later.
claims.supporting_passage: "Low versus high in-hospital mobility was associated with worse basic functional status at discharge (adjusted odds ratio (AOR)=18.03, 95% confidence interval (CI)=7.68-42.28) and at follow-up (AOR=4.72, 95% CI=1.98-11.28) and worse IADLs at follow-up (AOR=2.00, 95% CI=1.05-3.78)." ... "Forty-six percent of participants had declined in ADLs at discharge and 49% at follow-up; 57% had declined in IADLs at follow-up."
claims.pico_timeframe: 525 acute medical patients 70+ admitted for a non-disabling condition, Israel; exposure in-hospital mobility level (low vs high); outcome decline from premorbid ADL/IADL at discharge and 1 month; adjusted odds ratios.
claims.safe_wording: In an Israeli study of 525 people aged 70 and over, those who moved least in hospital were more likely to have lost everyday abilities at discharge and a month later, even after allowing for how unwell they were. This link does not prove that lying in bed caused the loss.
claims.qualifications: Observational; do not quote or convert the odds ratios for the public. Reverse causation possible.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found beyond the observational design.

numbers.meaning: patients 70+, one Israeli teaching hospital

claims.claim: In a randomised trial, a hospital walking programme helped older patients keep how far they got around their community a month after discharge, but made no difference to basic daily activities.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Patients in the MP group were assisted with ambulation up to twice daily, and a behavioral strategy was used to encourage mobility. Patients in the UC group received twice-daily visits." ... "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "The MP patients were seen up to twice a day for 15 to 20 minutes each session 7 days a week." ... "The MP group completed 122 of the potential 238 walks (51.3%)." ... "Although this is a small study that needs replication".
claims.location: Abstract, Interventions and Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment, Hospital MP), Results and Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 100 cognitively intact medical inpatients 65+ (97% men) able to walk before admission, one US VA hospital, 2010 to 2011; intervention assisted walking up to twice daily plus goal setting; comparator twice-daily attention visits; outcomes self-reported ADL and Life-Space Assessment 1 month after discharge.
claims.safe_wording: In one small US trial of 100 older veterans, helping people walk up to twice a day in hospital, with daily goals for time out of bed, did not change their basic daily activities. A month after going home, those who had the walking programme were getting about as far beyond their front door as before admission, while the usual-care group had lost about 10 points on a 120-point scale of how far and how often they went out.
claims.qualifications: 97% men, one veterans' hospital, cognitively intact, median stay 3 days; the originally registered main outcome (time out of bed) could not be measured, so these results come from other planned aims; only about half of offered walks happened; needs replication. Frame the family question around 'What is the walking plan for today?', not pressure to walk: some patients should not walk without help (the programme told patients not to walk without nursing help where needed).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Falls: 3 falls in 2 usual-care patients and none in the programme group; numbers too small to claim a safety benefit.

numbers.meaning: mean Life-Space Assessment score (0 to 120) 1 month after discharge, walking programme vs usual care
fall in life-space score in the usual-care group from admission to 1 month
patients randomised, 97% men
offered walks completed in the programme group

claims.claim: The Life-Space Assessment asks how far a person has moved from their bedroom out to beyond their town in the past 4 weeks, how often, and with what help.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2009 (Ann Intern Med) full text: "The LSA measures mobility during the four weeks preceding the assessment by asking about movement to specific life-space levels ranging from within one’s dwelling to beyond one’s town (–). Frequency of movement and use of assistance, either from equipment or another person, were assessed. Specifically, participants were asked: “During the past 4 weeks, have you: 1) been to other rooms in your home besides the room where you sleep; 2) been to an area outside your home such as your porch, deck, or patio, hallway of an apartment building, or garage; 3) been to places in your neighborhood other than your own yard or apartment building; 4) been to places outside your neighborhood, but within your town; and 5) been to places outside your town?”" ... "Life-Space composite scores ranged from 0 to 120 with higher scores representing greater mobility." Baker 2003: "The LSA assessed the range, independence, and frequency of movement over the 4 weeks preceding assessments." Brown 2016: "Life-space levels range from within one’s bedroom to beyond one’s town."
claims.location: Brown 2009 full text, Methods (Life-Space Mobility); Baker 2003 abstract, Measurements; Brown 2016 full text, Methods
claims.pico_timeframe: Measurement instrument; community-living older adults, Alabama.
claims.safe_wording: A life-space assessment asks about the past 4 weeks: have you been to other rooms of your home, outside your door (porch, garden, garage or landing), around your neighbourhood, elsewhere in your town, and beyond your town? It also asks how often and whether you needed a stick, frame or another person. Scores run from 0 to 120.
claims.qualifications: UK wording of the zones ('garden', 'landing') is a plain translation of the US questions; keep the five levels in the same order. Self-reported.

numbers.meaning: life-space levels beyond the bedroom
recall period
composite score range

claims.claim: Standard daily-living scales count self-care tasks done in and around the home (washing, dressing, eating, toilet, getting in and out of bed or a chair, walking across a room).
claims.supporting_passage: Loyd 2020: "Included studies used the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living or Barthel Index to measure ADL." ... "self-care (bathing, dressing, using the toilet, and eating) and mobility (transferring from bed or a chair, walking across the room)." Brown 2016: "Participants were asked at baseline to rate their ability to perform basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, feeding, toileting, grooming, transferring, and walking)".
claims.location: Loyd full text, Methods and Introduction; Brown 2016 full text, Methods (Functional Outcome Assessment)
claims.safe_wording: The usual daily-living scores count whether you can wash, dress, eat, use the toilet, get in and out of bed or a chair, and walk across a room. They do not ask whether you get to the shop, the bus stop or a friend's house.
claims.qualifications: Some versions add walking or grooming; describe the items, not every version.

claims.claim: In a small randomised trial, a hospital walking programme showed no difference on a daily-living scale but a difference in life-space a month after discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "For all periods, groups were similar in ability to perform ADL; however, at 1-month after hospitalization, the LSA score was significantly higher in the MP (LSA score, 52.5) compared with the UC group (LSA score, 41.6) (P = .02). For the MP group, the 1-month posthospitalization LSA score was similar to the LSA score measured at admission. For the UC group, the LSA score decreased by approximately 10 points." Full text: "For all periods, groups were similar in their ability to perform ADL (= .62); furthermore, ability to perform ADL did not significantly change over time (= .77), and there were no significant group-time interactions (= .76)." ... "Our initial trial registration described time out of bed using accelerometers as our primary outcome. However, technical failures in this measure precluded use of accelerometer data. Therefore, this report focuses on outcomes from other aims in the protocol." ... "In addition, the study was not powered to see significant ADL changes." ... "An example of a 10-point decrease would be an older person who previously reported no assistance to go into town 1 to 3 times a week (LSA score, 64) but who now requires a cane to go into town and goes less than once a week (LSA score, 54)."
claims.location: Abstract, Results; full text, Methods (Hospital Mobility Assessment), Results and Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 100 medical inpatients 65+ (97% men), one US VA hospital; walking programme vs attention control; Katz-type ADL and LSA 1 month after discharge.
claims.safe_wording: In a small US trial of 100 older veterans, a hospital walking programme made no difference to daily-living scores, which barely changed in either group. The life-space measure did pick up a difference: a month after discharge, people who had usual care had lost about 10 points, for example going from getting into town unaided 1 to 3 times a week to needing a stick and going less than once a week, while the walking group stayed close to where they started.
claims.qualifications: Do not say 'the choice of measure decided whether the programme looked useful' as a finding. Life-space was not the trial's registered primary outcome (time out of bed, which failed technically), so present this as one small trial that needs replication. The daily-living scale did not change in either group, so it could not show a difference; the trial was not powered for it. 97% men, cognitively intact, one veterans' hospital. For practitioner versions, name the registered-outcome issue.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single small trial; 6 of 50 programme patients and 2 of 50 usual-care patients did not complete; imputation and complete-case analyses agreed.

numbers.meaning: mean LSA score (0 to 120) at 1 month, walking programme vs usual care
LSA fall in usual care, admission to 1 month after discharge; programme group similar to admission
authors' worked example of a 10-point fall

claims.claim: After an emergency medical admission, older people's life-space falls and, on average, does not recover over up to two years.
claims.supporting_passage: "Immediately after hospitalization, covariate-adjusted LSA scores decreased in non-surgical patients by 10.31 points (95% CI −14.30 to −6.32) and in surgical patients by 22.45 points (95% CI −29.91 to −14.99)." ... "Indeed, LSA score recovery after non-surgical hospitalizations was non-significantly different from the null (average recovery of 0.66 points [95% CI −0.60 to 1.91] per log week). For example, at 12 weeks post-discharge, life-space recovered by an average of 1.69 points in non-surgical patients and by 13.80 points in surgical patients. As illustrated in, on average, within up to two years of the incident non-surgical hospitalization, these patients did not recover to their pre-hospital levels of life-space."
claims.pico_timeframe: 687 community-living Medicare beneficiaries 65+, central Alabama; 167 non-surgical and 44 surgical hospitalisations; life-space before and after, modelled from 6-monthly interviews; adjusted for age, sex, race, rural status, comorbidity and baseline ADL problems.
claims.safe_wording: In a US study that followed older people living at home, those admitted to hospital for a medical (non-surgical) reason lost about 10 points of life-space on average and, as a group, had not got back to their earlier level up to two years later. People admitted for surgery lost more at first but recovered within about a year.
claims.qualifications: Observational; averages hide individual variation; life-space was reported every 6 months, so the before and after values are model estimates; 'non-surgical' was self-reported and broad. Not 'caused by' hospital: say 'after' or 'linked with'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Underlying illnesses such as heart failure may explain part of the lack of recovery (authors' discussion).

numbers.meaning: adjusted average life-space fall after a non-surgical admission (0 to 120 scale)
adjusted average fall after a surgical admission
average recovery by 12 weeks, non-surgical vs surgical
non-surgical admissions analysed

claims.claim: A smaller life-space is linked with a higher risk of death and of moving into a care home.
claims.supporting_passage: Boyle 2010: "In a proportional hazards model adjusted for age, sex, race, and education, a more-constricted life space was associated with a greater risk of death (hazard ratio=1.18, 95% confidence interval=1.09-1.27, P<.001)" ... "This association persisted after the addition of terms for several potential confounders, including physical activity, performance-based physical function, disability, depressive symptoms, social networks, body mass index, and number of chronic medical conditions." Mackey 2014: "In multivariable-adjusted models, there was a strong linear trend between decreasing life-space and increasing risk of noncancer mortality (P = .005)." Watanabe 2022: "We found a negative association between LSM score and overall mortality even after adjusting for confounders". Sheppard 2013: "Over 6 years, the odds of NH admission increased 2% for every one point lower baseline life-space score independent of previously recognized risk factors."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-living older adults: Chicago 1,445 without dementia (mean 4.1 years); 3,892 US men 71 to 98 (2.7 years); 10,014 Japanese adults 65+ (median 5.3 years); 1,000 Alabama Medicare beneficiaries (6 years, nursing home admission); all observational, adjusted.
claims.safe_wording: In studies in the US and Japan, older people whose life-space was smaller were more likely to die in the following years, and in an Alabama study more likely to move into a nursing home, even after allowing for other health problems. These links do not show that shrinking life-space itself causes these outcomes; it may be a sign of declining health.
claims.qualifications: Associations only. Do not convert the hazard or odds ratios into 'times more likely' or absolute risks. Do not use Mackey's crude 41.2% vs 2.4% (only 34 men in the lowest group).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Watanabe 2022 found an L-shaped relationship: little further difference in mortality above a score of about 60.

numbers.meaning: cohort sizes (Boyle, Mackey, Watanabe, Sheppard)

candidates.reason: The core statistic is supported by the Loyd 2020 meta-analysis (30% pooled; 33% when restricted to studies with a baseline 2 weeks before admission, which answers the judge's concern about mixed baselines). Covinsky 2003 adds an optional age gradient. The first-hour checklist is judgement and must be presented as a practical suggestion, not a tested tool. The toilet, chair and bed map onto the basic daily activities the studies measured; the key, step and kettle do not. NICE NG27 could not be opened, so the post should not cite NICE; the ask-the-therapist step rests on Lockwood 2015 (occupational therapists do pre-discharge home visits; low to moderate quality evidence) and is advice, not a claim of entitlement. Follows editor guidance: no hip-fracture readiness framing from E109.

Boyd 2008 supports the 12-month outcomes and the one-month split, but the study measured being back to the usual level of self-care by one month, not whether recovery had 'started', so the core insight and opening line must change. Boyd also shows 38% of eventual recoveries came after the first month, which the post must state so that a family is not told the outcome is settled at one month. The one-month review is judgement; no evidence here that a review changes outcomes. Hardy and Gill 2004 is supported but concerns community disability from any cause and should be left out or clearly labelled, not placed beside Boyd's figures. Data are US, 1993 to 1998.
candidates.revised_angle: Being back to usual self-care a month after an emergency medical admission is a strong sign for the year ahead (in a US study, 56 in 100 of those back at one month were still at their usual level at a year, versus 17 in 100 of those who were not). But about 4 in 10 of the people who did recover got there after the first month, so the one-month point is a time to check and plan, not a verdict. Suggest (as judgement) asking for a review of walking and daily activities about four weeks after discharge.

candidates.reason: Time in bed is supported by Brown 2009 (45 US veterans, 83% of measured time lying; 35 of 45 able to walk a short distance on their own) with a second, non-veteran source as the judge asked (Pedersen 2013, Denmark, median 17 hours a day lying). Zisberg 2011 supports the association with worse function (observational). Brown 2016 supports the trial result only with its limits stated, including that the registered primary outcome could not be measured. The family question should be 'What is the walking plan for today?' so it prompts a plan rather than pressure to walk. Note: C01-05 (falls-rate angle, C01-B2) uses the same Brown 2009 and Pedersen figures; if both are published, avoid leading both with the 83% figure.

The life-space definition, the daily-living scale items and the associations with death and care home admission are supported (Brown 2009 full text, Baker 2003, Boyle 2010, Mackey 2014, Watanabe 2022, Sheppard 2013). The Brown 2016 numbers are correct, but the full text confirms the judge's concern: life-space was not the registered primary outcome (time out of bed by accelerometer, which failed technically), and the ADL scale did not change in either arm (not powered for it). So 'the choice of measure decided whether the programme looked useful' overstates one small trial. Brown 2009 (Ann Intern Med) gives stronger, independent support for the measurement point: after a medical admission, life-space fell about 10 points and did not recover over up to two years.
candidates.revised_angle: Daily-living scores ask whether you can wash, dress, use the toilet and cross a room; a life-space assessment asks how far beyond your front door you went in the past 4 weeks, how often, and with what help. After a medical admission, older people in a US community study lost about 10 points of life-space on average and, as a group, had not recovered it up to two years later. In one small trial, a hospital walking programme showed no difference on daily-living scores (which barely changed in either group) while life-space fell in usual care but not with the programme; this needs replication and life-space was not the trial's first-registered outcome. Position (judgement): rehabilitation services and trials should also count how far people get beyond the front door. Give readers the plain question: 'In the last 4 weeks, how far from your front door did you get, and how often?'
